svg.aria-label: flint-passthrough: a tenant pod declares a CSI inline volume naming a FlintPassthroughMount in its own namespace. The privileged node plugin resolves the CR, authorizes the pod's ServiceAccount, opens /dev/fuse, calls mount(2) itself and passes the file descriptor over a socket to an unprivileged worker pod running unchanged mount-s3. The bucket is mounted as-is with no flint control namespace. Privilege lands in three places, none of them the tenant namespace.
svg.text: Tenant namespace
PodSecurity: restricted — and it stays that way
the tenant pod
volumes:
- name: data
csi:
driver: s3.csi.chert.us
volumeAttributes:
chert.us/mount: datasets
that is the whole integration. Nine lines of pod spec.
No sidecar. No label. No webhook. No credential.
No privileged container. No mount propagation.
`spec.volumes[*].csi` is on the restricted allow-list.
FlintPassthroughMount — in the POD'S namespace
bucket · keyPrefix · endpoint · readOnly · uid · consumers
NodePublish
Volume
s3.csi.chert.us — the node DaemonSet
ONE privileged process per node. Not per pod, and never in a tenant namespace.
resolve
the CR named by volumeAttributes, in the TOKEN's namespace
authorize
the pod's kubelet-asserted ServiceAccount must be listed in
spec.consumers.serviceAccounts — ABSENT MEANS DENY
mount
it opens /dev/fuse and calls mount(2) ITSELF — the one act
that genuinely needs privilege, done once, in one place
hand off the fd
the FUSE file descriptor goes to the worker over SCM_RIGHTS
bind the result into the pod
one Bidirectional view of the kubelet directory — a private
view would lose every mount on a plugin roll
It holds NO S3 credential and has NO Secrets RBAC anywhere.
/dev/fuse fd
the worker pod — UNPRIVILEGED
in a system namespace, one per mounted volume
an unchanged `mount-s3` serves the fd it was given
non-root · every capability dropped · seccomp RuntimeDefault
read-only rootfs · no ServiceAccount token · no hostPath
The mounter needs no privilege because the mount(2)
ALREADY HAPPENED. That is the entire trick.
Credentials arrive on a loopback door, never as pod env.
flint-s3-broker — the only standing credential
and it says so: every issuance is a TokenReview-verified,
registration-bound, consumer-checked grant with an audit
line (ns, sa, pod-uid, cr, expiry)
TokenReview is ONLINE, not offline JWKS: a deleted pod's
token is refused within 60 s of its deletionTimestamp.
Offline verification would honour it all the way to `exp`.
It never reads a tenant Secret. Keys are short-lived.
S3 — and it is just S3
This is the one front end that writes NO control namespace at all.
<prefix>/<key>
Objects appear as files and nothing else is written — no manifest, no epoch cell,
no claim, no publish boundary. A prefix somebody else's tooling already owns stays
exactly as it was, which is precisely the point of this front end.
Durability, consistency and access control are S3's, unmediated. flint adds none and removes none.
What a passthrough mount is NOT
every one of these is a design decision, not a gap waiting to be filled
It is not POSIX.
No rename, no append, no in-place modification — at any setting.
It is not coordinated.
Two pods on one prefix do not see each other. There is nothing to see with.
It is not per-user.
The mount presents as ONE uid — NodePublish never sees the pod's securityContext.
It is not self-healing.
If the mounter dies, running containers are stranded on ENOTCONN; recreate the pod.
Where the privilege went — the accounting, said plainly
The webhook this replaced put a privileged container into every tenant pod. Privilege did not disappear; it was concentrated, the way Istio's CNI move concentrated it.
flint-s3-csi-node — privileged
One pod per node. It needs /dev/fuse and a Bidirectional
mount of /var/lib/kubelet, and the API server permits that
mode on privileged containers only.
It may create and delete pods in ONE namespace, and — with
the admission policy — only on its own node.
worker pods — unprivileged
One per mounted volume, in the workers namespace.
The namespace carries the PodSecurity `privileged` label
ONLY because hostPath is baseline-forbidden — the
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is the real guard.
Read the label as a formality, and the policy as the fence.
the tenant pod — nothing
It is given no privilege, no credential and no flint code.
Its ServiceAccount identity is asserted by kubelet, which
the pod cannot forge, and checked by the broker online.
This is the same chain flint-lean uses. The two front ends
differ in what runs in the worker, not in who is trusted.
